sources.title: District-level Climate Risk Assessment for India: Mapping Flood and Drought Risks released
sources.organization: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Science and Technology, Government of India
sources.temporal_coverage: District risk analysis uses flood and drought hazard records from 1970–2019; summary released December 2024.
sources.methodology: Government release summarizing a district assessment by IIT Mandi, IIT Guwahati and CSTEP.
sources.limitations: Risk bands are comparative; the release summarizes rather than reproduces the underlying report.

sources.title: How Extreme Heat is Impacting India: Assessing District-level Heat Risk
sources.organization: Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW)
sources.temporal_coverage: District heat trends for 1982–2022; socio-economic and health indicators include Census 2011 and NFHS 2019–21.
sources.methodology: CEEW district heat-risk index using 35 hazard, exposure and vulnerability indicators.
sources.limitations: Relative bands, dated indicators; state findings need validation.

sources.title: Mitigating the Urban Heat Island Effect in Indian Cities
sources.organization: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, Government of India
sources.temporal_coverage: HAP status reported July 2026; Delhi climate vulnerability assessment uses 1991–2020 observations and projections to mid-century.
sources.methodology: Ministry press release summarizing heat-action-plan status and the Delhi SAPCC 2.0 assessment.
sources.limitations: Ministry-reported plan counts and planned measures do not establish effectiveness or completed outcomes.

sources.title: NHRC calls for preventive measures by 11 States to protect vulnerable people from heat waves
sources.organization: National Human Rights Commission of India
sources.temporal_coverage: Heat risks and NCRB death data for 2018–2022; NHRC intervention issued May 2025.
sources.methodology: NHRC press release describing its communication to state governments and cited NCRB figures.
sources.limitations: The reported death count is attributed to NCRB; NHRC's requested measures are not evidence of implementation.

sources.title: Climate and Gender: Association Between Droughts and Intimate Partner Violence in India
sources.organization: American Journal of Epidemiology / National Library of Medicine PubMed Central
sources.temporal_coverage: National Family Health Survey rounds 2015–2016 and 2019–2021; article published November 2023.
sources.methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of 122,696 married women, combining survey IPV reports with precipitation-based and government socioeconomic drought classifications.
sources.limitations: Self-reported and cross-sectional data limit generalizability and causal inference; household income pathway was not tested.

claims.paraphrase: The district assessment placed 51 districts in very high and 118 in high flood-risk bands; about 85% of those districts are in Assam, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Gujarat, Odisha and Jammu and Kashmir.
claims.limitations: Risk classes are comparative, based on hazard, exposure and vulnerability, not absolute probabilities.

claims.paraphrase: The assessment placed 91 districts in very high and 188 in high drought-risk bands; more than 85% of these districts are in Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, West Bengal, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Chhattisgarh, Kerala, Uttarakhand and Haryana.
claims.limitations: Risk classes are comparative; the source summarizes the report rather than reproducing its full methods.

claims.paraphrase: Among the 50 districts with highest flood risk and 50 with highest drought risk, 11 were very high risk for both, including Patna, Alappuzha, Charaideo, Dibrugarh, Sibsagar, South Salmara-Mankachar, Golaghat, Kendrapara, Murshidabad, Nadia and Uttar Dinajpur.
claims.limitations: Examples are comparative index results, not forecasts of a particular event.

claims.paraphrase: CEEW classed 417 of 734 districts (57%), home to 76% of residents, at high or very high heat risk; Delhi, Maharashtra, Goa, Kerala and Gujarat ranked among the highest-risk states.
institutions: Council on Energy, Environment and Water
claims.limitations: The index uses 1982–2022 hazard data and older census and health inputs; categories are relative, not no-risk/risk absolutes.

claims.paraphrase: Comparing 2012–2022 with 1982–2011, CEEW found extra warm nights per summer in Mumbai (15), Bengaluru (11), Bhopal and Jaipur (7 each), Delhi (6) and Chennai (4); warm nights rose faster than hot days.
institutions: Council on Energy, Environment and Water
claims.limitations: Study comparison covers historical periods and is not an event attribution analysis.

claims.paraphrase: CEEW found high heat vulnerability in districts of seven named states, where heat combined with chronic illness, older people and under-fives; Odisha districts with green cover and blue infrastructure had lower vulnerability.
institutions: Council on Energy, Environment and Water
claims.limitations: State and district patterns use the study's historical indicator base and require local validation.

claims.paraphrase: By July 2026, heat action plans were reported for 23 states, 195 districts and 64 cities; national guidance recommends that plans protect street vendors and other outdoor workers through shade, hydration, cooling spaces, flexible hours and alerts.
claims.limitations: The release reports plan coverage and recommended measures, not their implementation quality or effects.

claims.paraphrase: Delhi's SAPCC 2.0 assessment identifies South Delhi as most and New Delhi as least climate-vulnerable; it projects higher summer maximum temperatures and more very hot days by mid-century, with cool roofs, cooling corridors, green infrastructure, drainage and wetland measures envisaged.
claims.scenario: The release reports about +1.5°C under SSP2-4.5 and up to +2.1°C under SSP5-8.5 by mid-century.
institutions: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
claims.limitations: Projection and vulnerability rankings are summarized from a state assessment; listed measures are planned, not evaluated outcomes.

claims.paraphrase: NHRC cited 3,798 NCRB-recorded heat and sun-stroke deaths in 2018–2022 and identified economically weaker people, outdoor workers, older people, children and homeless people as at risk from inadequate shelter and resources; it urged 11 states to provide protections.
claims.limitations: NHRC's recommendations do not establish whether states implemented them; the mortality figure is attributed to NCRB.

claims.locator: Article, abstract lines 98–101; results lines 260–263; discussion lines 308–312 and 318.
claims.paraphrase: In a national sample of 122,696 married women, socioeconomic drought status was associated with higher adjusted odds of physical, sexual and emotional IPV (1.34, 1.49 and 1.41); precipitation-based drought was associated with physical and emotional IPV (1.05 and 1.10). The authors note that their cross-sectional study cannot establish causality or test the income pathway.
claims.limitations: Cross-sectional survey associations do not prove a causal effect; the authors lacked prior-year household income and consumption data to test the proposed pathway.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The authors directly report drought-associated IPV odds, while stating that their design cannot establish causality or verify a mechanism.

search_audit.outcome: Opened Government of India district flood/drought assessment summary and CEEW district heat-risk report; retained named districts, states and differentiated groups.

search_audit.outcome: Opened a peer-reviewed national study reporting drought-associated intimate-partner-violence odds; association, not causality, is recorded.

search_audit.outcome: Search and direct MHA page attempt did not yield a substantive passage linking conflict to climate exposure or climate-adaptation access; no reverse link is asserted.

search_audit.query: India heat action plan district adaptation resilience urban heat mitigation government local capacity heat workers
search_audit.outcome: Opened Government of India heat-action-plan status and NHRC worker/community protection guidance; CEEW identifies risk-assessment gaps and Odisha green/blue infrastructure associated with lower vulnerability.

gaps: A peer-reviewed national study provides explicit drought–intimate-partner-violence associations but cannot establish causality or test the proposed household-income pathway; this is not evidence of an armed-conflict pathway.
The reviewed material does not directly establish that conflict or insecurity changes climate exposure or blocks adaptation access.
District heat classifications use 1982–2022 hazard data with older Census and NFHS indicators; they should not be read as a refreshed 2026 risk inventory.
